name: Science Quest — Year 9 Bank (50)
description: Biology 18 · Physics 16 · Chemistry 16. Created by Mrs Sarra Ben Amara.

questions.prompt: Which gas do plants absorb during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use light energy to turn it (with water) into glucose. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis requires light energy.
questions.explanation: True. Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which powers the reaction: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: Plants absorb carbon dioxide (CO₂) from the atmosphere through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata.
questions.text: Plants absorb ___ dioxide from the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Which substance absorbs light energy in green plants?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts. It absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Photosynthesis releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: False. Photosynthesis REMOVES carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and releases oxygen. Respiration is the process that releases carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll).
questions.text: During photosynthesis, plants produce glucose and ___.

questions.prompt: Which process releases carbon dioxide during the breakdown of glucose in aerobic respiration?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released). The carbon dioxide returns to the atmosphere.

questions.prompt: Animals obtain carbon by eating plants or other animals.
questions.explanation: True. Animals cannot photosynthesise, so they get carbon compounds by feeding on plants or other animals.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: Decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste. Their respiration releases the carbon back into the air as carbon dioxide.
questions.text: Dead organisms are broken down by ___.

questions.prompt: Which is a major carbon store?
questions.explanation: Oceans are a major carbon store: carbon dioxide dissolves in sea water and carbon is locked in shells and sediments. Other stores include the atmosphere, living organisms, fossil fuels and limestone rocks.

questions.prompt: Match each process to its role in the carbon cycle.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the air; respiration returns it; feeding passes carbon along food chains; decomposition breaks down dead material so the carbon can be recycled.

pairs.right: Takes in carbon dioxide to make glucose

adapted.prompt: Which process takes in carbon dioxide to make glucose?

questions.prompt: Complete the carbon cycle by dragging the correct processes to the labelled boxes.
questions.explanation: CO₂ in the air → plants by photosynthesis; plants → rabbit by feeding; rabbit → CO₂ in the air by respiration; dead material → decomposers by decomposition.

adapted.prompt: Which process moves carbon from the air into plants?

questions.prompt: Carbon can be stored in the bodies of living organisms.
questions.explanation: True. Carbon is found in the carbohydrates, proteins and fats that make up living organisms, so living things are a carbon store.

questions.prompt: What happens to carbon when a rabbit eats grass?
questions.explanation: Carbon compounds in the grass are digested and used to build the rabbit’s body. Carbon is never destroyed; it is transferred along the food chain.
options: It moves from grass to rabbit

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: Respiration in plants, animals and decomposers releases carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. (Combustion of fuels also releases it.)
questions.text: Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere during ___.

questions.prompt: Which organisms play an important role in decomposition?
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers. They feed on dead material and release carbon dioxide through respiration.

questions.prompt: Decomposition helps recycle carbon in ecosystems.
questions.explanation: True. Decomposers break down dead organisms, returning carbon to the air (as CO₂) and nutrients to the soil.

questions.prompt: Arrange the stages in the order that carbon moves through this food chain.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide in the air is taken in by the plant (photosynthesis), the rabbit eats the plant, and the fox eats the rabbit (feeding).

questions.prompt: What is the formula for density?
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume (ρ = m / V). Its units are g/cm³ or kg/m³.

questions.prompt: Density describes mass per unit volume.
questions.explanation: True. Density tells you how much mass is packed into each unit of volume, e.g. each cm³.

questions.prompt: A block has a mass of 120 g and a volume of 40 cm³. Calculate its density.
questions.explanation: Density = mass ÷ volume = 120 g ÷ 40 cm³ = 3.0 g/cm³.

questions.prompt: Which instrument measures mass?
questions.explanation: A balance measures mass (in g or kg).

questions.prompt: A liquid has a density of 2 g/cm³ and a volume of 50 cm³. Calculate its mass.
questions.explanation: Mass = density × volume = 2 g/cm³ × 50 cm³ = 100 g.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: The SI unit of density is kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³). g/cm³ is also commonly used but is not the SI unit (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³).
questions.text: The SI unit of density is ___.

adapted.prompt: What is the SI unit of density?

questions.prompt: A material has a mass of 240 g and a density of 8 g/cm³. Calculate its volume.
questions.explanation: Volume = mass ÷ density = 240 g ÷ 8 g/cm³ = 30 cm³.

questions.prompt: An object with a lower average density than water will normally float in water.
questions.explanation: True. Water has a density of about 1 g/cm³. Objects with a lower average density float; objects with a higher density sink.

questions.prompt: Water rises from 35 mL to 62 mL when a stone is submerged. Find the stone’s volume.
questions.explanation: Volume of stone = volume of water displaced = 62 mL − 35 mL = 27 mL = 27 cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³).

adapted.prompt: Water rises from 35 mL to 62 mL when a stone is added. What is the stone’s volume?

questions.prompt: Which method measures the volume of an irregular stone?
questions.explanation: Lower the stone into a measuring cylinder of water. The rise in water level equals the stone’s volume.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its description.
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter (g, kg); volume is the space it takes up (cm³, m³); density is mass ÷ volume; temperature measures how hot or cold something is (°C).

pairs.right: Measure of how hot or cold something is

questions.prompt: A rectangular block measures 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm and has a mass of 180 g. Find its density.
questions.explanation: Volume = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cm³. Density = 180 g ÷ 60 cm³ = 3.0 g/cm³.

questions.prompt: Which instrument measures temperature?
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature, usually in °C.

questions.prompt: Heat and temperature mean exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: False. Temperature (°C) measures how hot or cold something is. Heat is thermal energy (J) transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one.

questions.prompt: Match each method of thermal energy transfer to its description.
questions.explanation: Conduction: particles pass energy to neighbours (mainly in solids). Convection: warmer, less dense fluid rises and carries energy. Radiation: infrared waves, which need no particles and can travel through space.

pairs.right: Energy transfer through direct interactions between particles
Energy transfer through movement of liquids or gases

questions.prompt: How does thermal energy from the Sun reach Earth?
questions.explanation: Space is almost a vacuum, so there are no particles for conduction or convection. The Sun’s energy reaches Earth by radiation (electromagnetic waves).

questions.prompt: Which particle has a positive charge?
questions.explanation: Protons are positive (+1), electrons are negative (−1) and neutrons have no charge.

questions.prompt: Neutrons have no electrical charge.
questions.explanation: True. Neutrons are neutral. They are found with protons in the nucleus.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: The nucleus is at the centre of the atom. It contains protons and neutrons and holds almost all of the atom’s mass.
questions.text: The centre of an atom is called the ___.

questions.prompt: Which particles occupy electron shells?
questions.explanation: Electrons occupy shells (energy levels) around the nucleus.

questions.prompt: The atomic number equals the number of protons in an atom.
questions.explanation: True. The atomic number (proton number) is the number of protons, and it identifies the element.

questions.prompt: An atom has a mass number of 23 and an atomic number of 11. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 23 − 11 = 12. (This is sodium-23.)

questions.prompt: Who proposed the nuclear model following the gold foil experiment?
questions.explanation: Rutherford’s gold foil experiment (1911) showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus, which led to the nuclear model of the atom.

questions.prompt: Rutherford’s experiment showed that most of an atom is empty space.
questions.explanation: True. Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, so most of the atom must be empty space. A few bounced back off the small, dense nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which scientist introduced the model with electrons in fixed energy levels?
questions.explanation: Bohr (1913) proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed shells (energy levels).

questions.prompt: Arrange the electrons in the shells of a neutral sodium atom (atomic number 11).
questions.explanation: Sodium has 11 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second and 1 in the third → 2, 8, 1.

adapted.prompt: What is the electronic configuration of sodium (11 electrons)?

questions.prompt: Arrange the electrons in the shells of a neutral chlorine atom (atomic number 17).
questions.explanation: Chlorine has 17 electrons: 2 + 8 + 7 → 2, 8, 7.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with the correct word.
questions.explanation: Potassium’s symbol is K, from its Latin name kalium. (P is phosphorus.)
questions.text: The chemical symbol for potassium is ___.

questions.prompt: Which element has atomic number 8?
questions.explanation: Oxygen has 8 protons, so its atomic number is 8. (Carbon is 6, nitrogen 7, neon 10.)

questions.prompt: Match each symbol to its element name.
questions.explanation: Na = sodium (from Latin natrium), Mg = magnesium, Al = aluminium, Ca = calcium.

questions.prompt: A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons.
questions.explanation: True. The positive charges of the protons are balanced by the same number of negative electrons, so the atom has no overall charge.

questions.prompt: Arrange the electrons in the shells of a neutral calcium atom (atomic number 20).
questions.explanation: Calcium has 20 electrons: 2 + 8 + 8 + 2 → 2, 8, 8, 2.
